previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with HCV- and alcohol-related cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for acute confusion. She was found to have hepatic encephalopathy, likely due to non-adherence to her lactulose regimen and possible medication overuse, including oxycodone and Excedrin. Initial evaluation showed no acute intracranial, abdominal, or infectious processes on imaging and labs. Her mental status improved with q2h lactulose and temporary hold of sedating medications, which were gradually restarted. Headaches during admission were thought to be medication-overuse related and improved with regimen adjustment. She was discharged home with a visiting nurse for medication support, with instructions to maintain lactulose adherence and follow up with her primary and liver specialists.

#Toxic metabolic encephalopathy: Patient was found by daughter 
and PCP to be disoriented after not having a bowel movement for 
the past 2 days in the setting of only taking lactulose 
intermittently. Given h/o cirrhosis, physical exam findings of 
asterixis, along with impaired hepatic synthetic function, 
hepatic encephalopathy is the most likely cause of the patient's 
encephalopathy. Possible contribution from medications (patient 
took oxycodone and ambien the previous evening, both of which 
are hepatically cleared). Infection unlikely, as patient is 
afebrile, CXR clear, UA nitrate and leukocyte negative w/ few 
bacteria, though the UA culture was positive for alpha hemolytic 
colonies consistent with alpha streptococcus or Lactobacillus 
sp. No ascites or portal vein thrombus identified on US ON ___. 
Called PCP, who was surprised by oxycodone and ambien rx. A 
search of PMP revealed pt's podiatrist to be prescriber of 
record. Lactulose 30 mL PO/NG Q2H; titrated to ___ BM/day until 
clear mental status. Rifaximin 550 mg PO/NG BID continued. 
Decreased patient's home oxycodone to 5mg and avoid additional 
sedating medications and recommend oxycodone and ambien not be 
prescribed following taper in this patient, given hepatic 
clearance of these medications. Taper discussed below. 

#Cirrhosis w/ evidence of synthetic dysfunction (INR 1.50) w/ 
ascites: Patient has right upper quadrant tenderness, AST 54, 
ALT 30, Alk phos 149, Tbili 1.2, albumin 3.0, ___ 16.3, PTT 35.7, 
INR 1.5 (1.4-1.8 at baseline), suggestive of advanced liver 
cirrhosis consistent w/ clinical history of chronic hepatitis C, 
HCC, and alcohol abuse. Child Class B. Continued home 
spironolactone.

#RUQ Tenderness
In patient with cirrhosis and AMS, concerning for SBP though no 
ascites on U/S or CT. No fever. No rebound or guarding. S/P 
cholecystectomy. Liver edge palpable and tender, likely related 
to cirrhosis. U/S w/ Doppler today showed no ascites and patent 
portal vein.

#Hepatitis C. Continued home Harvoni 

#Leukopenia (WBC 2.3): WBC 1.4-3.5 at baseline in ___ in the 
setting of cirrhosis and likely hypersplenism. Should be 
followed as outpatient.  

#Thrombocytopenia (platelets 39,000): Platelets 40-80,000 at 
baseline in the setting of cirrhosis and likely hypersplenism. 
Should be followed as outpatient. 

#QT prolongation on EKG: Unchanged from patient's baseline. Will 
monitor closely and use QT prolonging medications cautiously 
though home medications were verified. F/u monitoring EKGs as a 
outpatient at discretion of PCP 

___ wound on left forearm: Reportedly occurred during a 
cooking accident. Offered daily wound care.

#Insomnia: Day/night reversal likely related to probable hepatic 
encephalopathy. Treated hepatic encephalopathy, as above. 
Continued home trazodone, monitoring sedation in the setting of 
toxic metabolic encephalopathy. QT interval was monitored closed 
while hospitalized, and should continue to monitor QT interval 
as outpatient.

#Bacteruria: Urine culture found to be growing alpha hemolytic 
colonies consistent with alpha streptococcus or Lactobacillus 
sp. Patient has no burning w/ urination or difficulty urinating. 
Does not require treatment at this time. 

#DM2: Last A1C 10.2% in ___, on home insulin. Continued home 
glargine 24u/24u with ISS. Continued gabapentin. 

#GERD: Continued home Omeprazole 

#Pain and numbness in right foot s/p ankle surgery (tendon 
tear). Home oxycodone dose reduced to 5mg q6h:prn (pain). Plan 
to dose reduce oxycodone by 50%/week with close outpatient 
follow-up to manage taper and monitor for withdrawal

#History of depression and psychiatric hospitalizations: 
Continued home duloxetine and quetiapine

#Restless Leg Syndrome: Continued home pramipexole

Transitional issues:
- Oxycodone should be tapered and ultimately should no longer be 
prescribed. A typical taper is to decrease the oxycodone dose by 
50% for 1 week (continuing to decrease by 50%/week thereafter) 
with close follow-up and monitoring for withdrawal. This may 
need to taper slower if withdrawal symptoms are significant. 
- Consider arranging orthopedics follow-up to manage pain, as it 
is reported to be related to a tendon rupture in her ankle. They 
may be able to provide a brace for stability and pain control. 
- QT interval was monitored closely during hospitalization, and 
the QTc was 439 on the day of discharge. Patient was kept on 
home medications, many of which are QT prolonging. Special care 
should be taken before uptitrating these medications or adding 
any additional QT prolonging medications. 
- If develops fever or urinary symptoms, should start empiric 
antibiotics for UTI. Bacteruria noted upon admission, and 
confusion was deemed to be related to hepatic encephalopathy, 
but if clinical status changes, we would recommend a low 
threshold for starting empiric antibiotics. 
- Insomnia: day/night reversal thought to be related to hepatic 
encephalopathy. If additional medications needed to treat true 
insomnia, should consider Benadryl rather than ambien (will have 
less impact on mental status).

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___, 

You were admitted to the hospital because you were confused, and 
your care team determined that the cause of your confusion was 
from a buildup of toxins in your body from your liver disease. 
It is very important that you take your lactulose as prescribed 
so that you have 3 bowel movements per day to help remove these 
toxins from your body. 

We also believe that the oxycodone and ambien that you were 
taking may have contributed to your confusion. These medications 
are processed by your liver, but because of your liver disease, 
the medications stay in your system longer and can lead to 
confusion. We are recommending that you stop taking the ambien 
and taper off of the oxycodone. 

It was a pleasure taking care of you, best of luck.
Your ___ healthcare team
